China|**21**| |The automotive sector|**22**| |Palladium investment|**23**| 2 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **19 April 2012** ## **Overview** Following two months of outright bullishness in the precious metals market, March provided a salutary lesson that prices do not move in straight lines as the prices of all four of the major metals softened. In fact, iridium was the only one of the precious metals which we watch which did not see its price fall, with ruthenium and rhodium losing ground too. The US Dollar strengthened a little during the month (particularly in the first two weeks) to place the precious metals complex under some pressure and contribute to this weakness. However, global economic issues dominated. Data from China showed a slowing economy there to weaken one of the driving forces behind the stronger prices of many commodities. At the same time, investors worried about the relative health of the US economy. Comments made by the US Federal Reserve in late February, throughout March and in early April indicated that while interest rates were unlikely to rise anytime soon, further quantitative easing was certainly not likely. This dented the optimism of many investors who trimmed their long positions, sending the metals lower regardless of fundamentals. Towards the end of the month, with the end of many companies’ financial years and the end of the quarter approaching, it would have taken a brave investor to go long and swim against the tide. Not enough brave investors could be found on this occasion and the prices of all of the metals sagged further in the second half of the month, ending March lower than they had been at its start (and suffering further at the start of April). It is, though, worth noting that, of the four major metals, only palladium lost ground in the first quarter of 2012. Even gold, whose performance has generally been seen as disappointing recorded gains of over 5 per cent in price terms while silver and platinum outperformed their sister metals with gains of more than fifteen per cent from the start of the year to the end of the first quarter. **_Figure 3_** _: The market seemed to find the rather larger Spanish debt question uninteresting during Q1 and may have underestimated sovereign risk as a result._ Spain is currently running a budget deficit and recent moves by the central Government to raise this year’s targeted deficit have worried the markets. Although the European Union managed to encourage the Spanish Government to reduce this slippage (i.e. to target a slightly lower deficit), this lack of absolute commitment to austerity made bond investors a touch more nervous than they had been previously. The new concern is that although Greece has been supported through bailouts and (in effect) a partial default on its bonds, the Spanish economy is much larger and it is not clear whether Europe has either the appetite or ability to rescue Spain if Spain cannot rescue itself. Austerity and a convincing move towards eliminating the budget deficit become of key importance in allowing Spain to roll over existing debt at bearable interest rates. However, Spain already has problems, with an unemployment rate above that of Greece with plenty of austerity (or expenditure cuts) still to come. Youth unemployment is higher still and there is real concern that the level of savings which would have to be made could 4 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **19 April 2012** be impractical in the current environment of weak consumer demand, poor employment and soft real estate prices. While we still believe the European debt crisis will be resolved successfully, the recent rise in Spanish bond yields and the market’s lack of appetite for them have made it clear that this will be a longer term process than some of the headline writers might have previously implied. **_Figure 5_** _: ...and Portuguese bond yields suggest that something is certainly not healthy in a low growth environment._ 5 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **19 April 2012** ### **The Fraser Institute Mining Survey** The Fraser Institute released its annual mining survey in the first quarter of 2012. This project questions a large number of mining executives to find their opinions on policy towards the mining industry and other relevant issues faced by miners in a wide range of jurisdictions. AS is usually the case, Canada was revealed as one of the best places for a mining company to operate. Unsurprisingly, uncertainty over government policy would be a serious deterrent to impediment to almost every respondent in Venezuela. Of greater concern for the platinum industry, is the fact that more than 90 per cent of respondents had similar concerns over investing in Zimbabwe. The equivalent figure for South Africa was nearly 70 per cent. In itself, this is worryingly large but over half of all respondents stated that they would not pursue investments at all in Zimbabwe due to this uncertainty whereas the equivalent figure for South Africa was only ten per cent. Interestingly, South Africa’s performance on this and some other questions was better than last year while Zimbabwe performed worse, as it becomes a less attractive jurisdiction in which to operate. We recommend the report to anyone interested in the operating environ

ment for mining. It can be found at https://www.fraserinstitute.org/uploadedFiles/fraser-ca/Content/ research-news/research/publications/mining-survey-2011-2012.pdf. 6 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **19 April 2012** ## **Gold** Since peaking at $1,785 on the 28th of February, the trajectory of the gold price has been downwards during March and the start of April. For the first quarter as a whole, gold gained 6.6 per cent in US Dollar terms moving from its opening $1,564 to $1,668. While this can be seen as a healthy recovery from the late December 2011 lows, sentiment towards the yellow metal has slowly soured as the European crisis has stopped making as many headlines, the Chinese economic miracle appears a little more fragile and the Indian Government has started to intervene in the gold market. **_Figure 5_** _: Is your glass half full or half empty?_ March would have been dispiriting for many investors. For the first two months of the year, gold bulls had been rewarded as the price of this metal soared from a low of $1,545 in late December to a high of $1,785 on February 28th . However, the slump lower on the final day of February set the tone for a weak March as the gold price slid slowly lower from an opening $1,697 to a closing $1,670 (and lower in early April). This decline has prompted a number of commentators to speculate on the possibility that gold’s bull run has already ended although we would not be so hasty. The heavy liquidation in gold at the end of February weighed on the market throughout March as investors fretted about gold’s new found price volatility. The initial moves in March were downwards as gold slipped to a low of $1,665 on the 6th of March under pressure from a strengthening US Dollar which was benefiting from a relatively benign outlook for the US economy. Iranian-Israeli political tension provided some support for gold and the price rallied above $1,700, reaching $1,715 on the 9th of March and passing the 200 day moving average en route. Continuing snippets of positive information on the US economic situation kept the Dollar firming until the middle of the month though and placed gold under pressure. It retreated to $1,645 on the 14th . Fears over a slowing Chinese economy encouraged increased sensitivity to risk amongst investors, driving many commodities lower. However, gold was relatively unaffected despite an Indian jewellers strike and, with concerns about Spanish sovereign debt reemerging, it managed to recover some ground to end the month at $1,668. It did not, however, challenge the $1,700 level, suggesting that whatever the longer term outlook for the price, there is certainly the potenti

al for further price falls in the short term. 7 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **19 April 2012** ### **Longer term price forecasts** While gold sentiment remains generally bullish based on negative real interest rates and expectations of heightened inflation in the coming years in many Western economies, the gold price has essentially moved sideways since October last year, marking a period of six months of disappointing price performance and prompting some investors to proclaim the end of gold’s bull run. We have previously commented on a typical price forecast for gold where the price is expected to rise in the following twelve to eighteen months before falling back towards support from the cost of production. This shape of price curve has been forecast by many in the market for most of the last decade. However, our current forecast sees some good reasons to remain bullish of gold in the longer term while remaining more concerned about the short term price outlook. Long term gold price support

**_Figure 8_** _: Are investors having to work harder for every successive upwards price movement?_ In the medium to longer term, however, there are still good reasons to own gold and for many investors to buy more. Firstly, it is not clear how robust the US economy really is. While it seems to be growing acceptably, the housing market remains depressed and unemployment is still stubbornly high so there is little room for tighter interest rates or other policy. The creaking European economy and slowing growth in China also pose a threat: the USA is not an island and slower global growth could yet drive further quantitative easing in the USA as well as in Europe. From a developed world perspective it is still not clear that there is any approach to excessive sovereign debt burdens other than default or encouraging higher inflation over an extended period of time. If inflation is still the preferred exit strategy for these countries, then any asset that can boast some inflation-proofing should still find willing buyers. We would argue that gold is not the best inflation hedge available but significant numbers of people do believe that gold can play this role and there should still be continued demand for gold in the coming years. Outside the developed world, the recent Wenzhou experiment might give us a glimpse of the future. In this, the Chinese Government has started to regularise the shadow banking system and to increase the amount of foreign investment that can be made. This can be seen as part of a range of moves to (gradually) liberalise the domestic economy. Currently, investors can only legally hold relatively small amounts of foreign currency and assets like gold can play an equivalent role to cash. Any increase in the ability to buy foreign assets is therefore negative for gold demand at some level. However, given the rapid speed of growth in China and the more sedate pace of reform of currency regulations, we expect Chinese demand for gold and other assets still to increase for a reasonable number of years, providing another reason to be bullish for gold in the longer term. 9 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **19 April 2012** ### **Indian import duty** As we previously reported, on January the 17th ,

the Indian Government duly announced that it was increasing the import duty on silver and gold. These duties were previously increased in February 2010 with very little impact on consumer buying behaviour. The January changes increased the import duty on gold from 300 Rupees per ten grams to two per cent of the gold value (currently roughly $33). For silver, duty was increased from 1,500 Rupees per kg to six per cent of the metal value (from roughly 90 US cents per ounce to closer to $2 at current prices). 

As we noted at that time, in the short term, addition of extra taxes is negative for metal demand both by increasing price sensitivity over the medium and longer term and by encouraging the deferral of purchases in the short term. We also commented that experience of government behaviour led us to believe that these duty levels were more likely to rise in the future than to fall. 

However, we did not expect duty rates to rise as quickly as they have. In mid-March (the 17<sup>th</sup> ), the Indian Government announced its plans to double the duty on gold imports again, with the rise likely to take effect from the first of April. On this occasion, the Government made clear the link between India’s current account deficit and this action. In addition to the increase in import duty, the Government has also proposed the imposition of a one per cent excise tax on non-branded gold jewellery and various other levels of excise tax on other gold products. (It has also moved to limit lending by non-banking finance companies which is collateralised against gold jewellery, bullion or coins). 

The immediate response of the jewellery sector has been a twelve day long strike in protest at these tax increases. The Government seems intent on imposing the duty increases but has shown some signs of a conciliatory attitude by indicating that it may look at the excise tax changes. With both sides keen to find some middle ground, we do not expect the strike to continue much longer. In the short term, this has meant a lack of physical support for the gold price during its recent weak spell. It currently seems that the Government will give way on the excise duty on jewellery and the strike will end in the first half of April. 

A Reuters survey of a (small) number of jewellery market participants forecast that Indian imports of gold could fall by 30 per cent this year, or roughly 300 tonnes, as a result of high prices, high levels of recycling and import duty increases. If this were to happen, this would significantly weaken one of the recent drivers of higher gold prices and would cause us to be less bullish over the outlook for gold. However, we expect the major impact of this duty increase to be short term and much smaller. While there will be some additional price elasticity of demand, we expect consumers and jewellery manufacturers to adjust fairly rapidly to these changes and that net demand losses will be much less significant than this. Over the longer te

rm, though, we fear that there may be further duty hikes, suggesting that there could be some continued erosion of Indian demand while the stubborn national current account deficit persists. Comments from the Bombay Bullion Association suggest that imports of gold into India may have fallen by four fifths year-on-year in March. 

Gold is not unpopular everywhere though. On the 14<sup>th</sup> of March, the Singaporean authorities announced their intention to increase the amount of gold trading taking place in the country. An estimated two per cent of world gold passes through Singapore presently according to the authorities who are planning to increase this to at least ten per cent. Precious metals are currently subject to a seven per cent duty when sold within Singapore and the current proposal is to remove this on investment grade metals (gold, silver and platinum) in order to increase trading volumes. Palladium does not currently seem to be included in this exemption.

### **Gold production** 

The market was reminded of the potential for supply side risks to disrupt the commodity markets by the mid-March coup which took place in Mali. Mali is a significant producer of primary (mined) gold so the direct impact on the gold market is limited. However, political instability in West Africa, which is a large producer of gold as a region, is more concerning. International pressure is being placed on the leaders of the coup to return power to the elected government and the possibility of sanctions being imposed has been raised. At the moment, there is no indication of interruptions to gold mining activity within the country, although we are aware that this situation could well change if the military rebels retain power. Even if disruption were to occur, there is likely to be little or no direct impact on the international gold price. 

However, this coup and the international response to it do raise two further issues: conflict gold and operational risk. 

The Dodd-Frank act has recently introduced and defined the concept of conflict gold. As the act stands, this refers to an attempt to prevent the production and sale of gold in the Democratic Republic of Congo and neighbouring countries from financing conflict. The act and resultant rules seem likely to encourage or (effectively) mandate more detailed chain of custody rules for many gold producers, refiners and consumers. The act’s main threat to gold supply is that, with a definition of conflict gold already in place, and audit procedures and chain of custody rules in existence, it may be extended relatively simply to cover new conflicts, preventing supply from some regions at times of crisis. 

While this may be morally correct, it is likely to add to operational risk for many mines. We have previously commented on resource nationalism and the addition of political risk (or even the reminder that politi

cal risk exists) can only add to producers’ and investors’ concerns. Given that an increasing amount of gold exploration and production is taking place in “non-vanilla” countries, new operations in such regions are likely to be subject to a greater discount on their value, making the investment decision for new operations more difficult and deterring new production or, effectively, increasing production costs. 

### **Official sector** 

The official sector has continued to be a buyer of gold so far this year. Data on gold reserves is typically released at least one month after any buying takes place. January 2012 data reveals that Belarus, Kazakhstan and Turkey all added to their gold holdings during the month (although the Turkish data may be complicated by the central bank’s decision to accept gold as collateral from commercial banks). February data revealed further significant buying by the Kazakh Central Bank too. Interestingly, the Russian Central Bank revealed a decrease in the weight of gold held within its reserves during February (although the official data on all central bank gold holdings is not one hundred per cent reliable). 

Although significant falls in central bank metal holdings have been unusual in the last few years, we do not believe that this marks a change in the attitude of central banks towards gold. Although the official sector holds a range of views towards gold, the overwhelming feeling towards many reserve currencies is one of concern over developed world debt burdens and the possibility that the value of their currencies might be eroded by inflation 

The attitude towards gold as an alternative reserveable asset is therefore a little more positive, ranging from close to neutral to a desire to purchase more gold. There is little desire evident in the official sector to reduce holdings. However, for a bank such as the Russian Central Bank which is known to be purchasing gold from domestic production, small fluctuations in metal holdings are not unusual (particularly in February, a month with an unusual number of days, which can disrupt regular shipments of metal). We believe that a large majority of central banks would like to maintain or increase their gold holdings.

Looking at the wider meaning of gold to governments is also interesting. Although there is no indication that China is buying gold to add to its reserves, it is certainly buying gold producers. As the example of India (mentioned above) indicates, gold can play a role like the new oil where producing countries benefit greatly in terms of exports as the price rises and importing countries suffer a worse balance of payment. So, gold buying can be political in countries which are not running an economic surplus. Although gold may be a reserveable asset, it is not exactly cash and its importation does negatively impact a country’s balance of payments. We expect th

e major official sector buyers in fact to be oil or commodity producers running a balance of payments surplus. 12 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **19 April 2012** ## **Silver** As with gold, the silver price had performed strongly during the first two months of 2012, soaring from $27.85 at the start of the year to a high of $36.91 on the 28th of February, an increase of almost a third. On a recent visit to Japan, we were explicitly told that many physical silver investors were interested in the short term gains that could be made in contrast to the more “buy and hold” philosophy of gold investors. Any who managed to take profits at this high point were proved right as silver slid lower in March, falling back to close to $32 an ounce, a retracement of approximately half of the gains that had previously been made. After the first half of January when silver outperformed gold, the gold:silver price ratio has remained relatively flat at close to 51:1. At the end of February, this dipped towards 49:1 as gold suffered a strong selloff. During March, though, gold steadily recovered compared to silver even as the prices of both metals fell, suggesting that some additional “safe haven” premium is still attached to gold. With gold prices relatively subdued it is thus no surprise that silver prices have softened. However, the interesting question is whether a silver price of roughly $32 is high or low. We give our thoughts on that below. Silver Price (USD/oz)

**_Figure 9_** _: Silver is flirting with the $32 level._ Whether the silver price is high or low, it was higher at the end of February than it was at the end of March. Silver had reached a high of roughly $37 on the 28th of February but had already fallen back to $34.68 at the end of that month. Daily moves of this size are problematic for investors, particularly when they hold positions on margin, and they erode confidence or the desire to invest. The market made a half-hearted attempt to rebound on the 1st of March, reaching a monthly high of $35.55 that day. It was unable to hold onto these gains given pressure from a firming Dollar. Some physical buying emerged from end users but a sharp reduction in speculative positioning depressed prices further, to $32.60 on the 6th of March. The Dollar continued firming until the middle of the month but gold found some support from Eurozone worries and silver, in turn, found support from gold. Nonetheless, the price sagged, slipping lower to a plateau near or just below $32 an ounce even as the Dollar relented briefly. With European debt issues coming back into the news, the Euro could come under further pressure and silver remains a li

ttle exposed to possible renewed downside pressure. 

### **What is a precious metal?** 

According to Wikipedia (which is not necessarily the store of all wisdom on the precious metals market admittedly), the answer to this question is that a precious metal is “a rare, naturally occurring metallic element of high economic value”. The problem with this definition is that at various times silver (and ruthenium) have not been amongst the 



13 

**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** 

**19 April 2012** 

### most expensive elements. 

So, it there a better definition of a precious metal? In our view, there are two potential approaches to this question which might work. One is simply to define precious metals by listing them. This argument is rather circular but means that gold, silver and platinum are simply precious metals because they have been defined as such for a long period of time. Palladium and the minor platinum group metals may qualify as precious metals in some consumers’ eyes but, being less well known are, in a way, less “precious”. The second approach is a behavioural one, of asking whether a particular person behaves as if a metal is precious. 

Using these two approaches gives different views as to whether the silver price is too high or too low. It is clear that the general public does believe that silver is a precious metal. In language terms, silver medals are understood to mean something of value and consumers are well aware of the value of silver. In some locations, such as India or South America, silver has often played a monetary role as an alternative not only to cash but to gold. 

Gold is universally the first precious metal that people think of but, with gold prices close to record nominal levels, gold is too expensive for some investors or poorer savers. For jewellery, where consumers might previously have bought nine carat gold alloys (37.5 per cent gold) when gold was trading below $300, the yellow metal’s price now makes that unattractive, something that can be seen from falling UK hallmarking figures for instance. Silver has taken up some of that slack with silver jewellery filling some gaps in jewellery collections or competing in the more “fashion” end of the market. Viewed in this light, the price of silver is less important than the high price of gold and silver may still be undervalued as a precious metal. 

From a behavioural perspective, silver is usually treated as a fully-fledged precious metal. Thieves know its value: antiques programmes in the UK often show members of the public delighted to be told their item is made of silver and then disappointed when they realise that it is worth less than they thought. We are interested, however, in the psychological impact of the $32 per ounce figure. This is relevant because it is equivalent to a one Dollar per gram price, or a thousand Dollars per kilogram. 

For many customers (and perhaps producers), we believe the $1 per gram level i

s important. The precious metals world itself is used to pricing materials in troy ounces. However, much of the rest of the world prices in pounds or in grams and kilograms. From the perspective of an industrial purchaser, a move over $1,000 per kilogram could change their behaviour, making them more sensitive to price movements than before. With the metal trading above this price, end user efforts to thrift and the desire for producers to hedge their output could be substantially greater than at lower levels. For the moment, $32 seems to be too high for some consumers but too low for investors. 

### **Photovoltaic demand** 

According to photovoltaic (PV) research consultancy solarbuzz, end-market revenues for photovoltaic equipment is set to fall from US$35.4 billion in Q4 2011 to $22 billion in Q4 2012. A delay in the reduction of German subsidies led to an unexpected boom in European installations during the first quarter of this year from consumers anxious to install systems while they were still heavily subsidised but demand for new panels is expected to lessen later in the year. 

However, this reduction in revenues will be driven by a fall in unit pricing due to industry overcapacity rather than by a drop in production. The market had previously been overly optimistic about consumer demand and had built excessive manufacturing capacity and also increased stockpiles of finished PV units. With much of this stockpile now absorbed by consumers, output should improve this year and return closer to real underlying consumer demand. Actual output of PV units looks set to increase in the first half of the year

Over the longer term, these price reductions within the photovoltaic industry should have a mixed effect on silver demand. Lower prices will lead to enhanced demand for photovoltaic systems. With silver-based thick film technology taking a substantial albeit decreasing share of the market, this will lead to additional silver demand both this year and next. However, falling prices will place pressure on margins throughout the industry. When silver was trading at $20 an ounce, the industry was expending significant amounts of effort to displace silver from PV technology or to come up with other alternatives. At the higher current prices, this thrifting or replacement can only become more intensive, threatening silver demand. If efforts at reducing silver loadings are not successful, then other PV technologies are likely to take market share due to lower material costs.

However

, we note that, according to a news report on the 22<sup>nd</sup> of February, April shipments of platinum from primary Impala production were likely to be reduced by half from their normal levels (this is in accordance with the processing time to produce platinum from primary ore). If the platinum market were to be particularly tight, this could lead to some upwards price pressure during the coming month. Impala also noted that it could take until the end of March to return underground ore production to normal levels. While there is some residual concern over relations between the two unions (the trigger for the strike), the situation currently appears to be stable. 

Further East on the Bushveld complex, Modikwa (a joint venture between ARM and Anglo American Platinum) saw strike action breaking out, this time over wages. The strike lasted for over three weeks with the loss of a little over 20,000 ounces of platinum group metals. At the same time, Samancor, the chrome miner, saw strikes at some of its South African operations. The industrial relations climate within South Africa remains more than challenging and we expect to see further losses of production due to strike action this year. 

### **Platinum production II - Southern African Government action** 

In March, the South African Government announced that it is to invest 3.4 billion Rand in platinum production based around the current Platmin Pilanesberg operation, the Sedibelo property and Magazynskraal. The Pilanesberg operation has a planned capacity of roughly 250,000 ounces of platinum group metals per annum but the new company has apparently targeted annual production of 1.1 million ounces of pgms in total within five years. The operations are all relatively shallow with some being open pit and development could be relatively rapid but we think this timescale and size of output are both extremely challenging to meet. 

One interesting issue with the project is that the new company plans to use a hydrometallurgical process rather than smelting in treating the ore to produce metal. If this were successful, this could remove some of the problems of treating high chrome content UG2 ore and it could also reduce energy usage, something that would be very useful in a South Africa which is currently facing electricity supply issues and will do so for some time to come. We do not have enough information on the process to assess its technical suitability for processing the platinum group metals but would caution that hydrometallurgical treatment of nickel laterite ores proved very significantly more difficult than had been thought at first. 

For this month, we have decided not to comment on progress in Zimbabwe’s ongoing indigenisation discussions. If you would like an updated view, please get in touch: otherwise we will return to this theme next month. 

### **The automotive sector** 

Although we remain relatively positive about the outlook for the platinum price, it has come under some p

ressure from the simple logical thought chain stretching from European recession to low car sales to low demand for platinum from diesel catalytic converters. Although diesel market share is rising and platinum demand from this subsector may perform better than the market expects, a slowing European market is clearly not a positive for platinum demand overall. News that French passenger car sales fell by nearly a quarter was rather unwelcome. At the same time, Spanish car sales dropped by 5 per cent. 

The French year-on-year change largely appears to be a result of the anniversary of the 



18

end of the previous incentive scheme for smaller cars and should therefore have been expected. These schemes also had the side-effect of lowering diesel market share since the incentives offered were more significant in percentage terms on smaller cars than on larger cars. Diesel passenger cars are typically larger than average and diesel market share was therefore depressed. So, although car sales dropped (and will drop for the year as a whole), the effect on platinum demand should be lower than the headline figure. 

Likewise, a decline in Spanish sales of five per cent should not be unexpected given the high levels of unemployment and the current austerity programmes, not to mention the multi-year trend of falling sales. Weakness in the Italian market is marked and unpleasant but not surprising (although March figures were negatively impacted by a truckers’ strike which affected production). 

In contrast, the fact that German car sales outperformed sales during March 2011 by 3.4 per cent gathered less attention. In our view, much of the weakness in the European car sector has already been factored into the platinum price and, unless there is a marked further deterioration from previous forecasts, we see more upside for demand than downside. 

Outside Europe, the picture for platinum demand for the diesel sector is positive. The Indian economy is still growing, albeit more slowly than desired, and the Government subsidy for this fuel is making diesel cars ever more popular, driving additional demand. Diesel fuel demand is rising by 8 per cent per year and the diesel engine’s share of new car sales is now above 50 per cent, having risen above that level for the first time in December. We feel that this fuel subsidy will eventually have to be reduced but as the Nigerian Government recently showed, removing subsidies is painful and can take a lot of effort and time. 

Elsewhere, tougher emissions limits will be imposed on light duty diesel trucks sold in Brazil from the start of 2013. The introduction of new sulphur fuel will also allow the fitment of more advanced catalytic aftertreatment to heavier vehicles on the same timescale, adding a touch more platinum demand. More negatively, China recently announced that the diesel China IV emissions rules which were schedu

led for implementation in early 2012 have been delayed to July 2013 due to a lack of low sulphur fuel. ### **Chinese platinum jewellery** A recent flying visit to Shenzhen in China gave us the opportunity to speak to a number of the manufacturers of platinum (and palladium) jewellery. We are happy to be able to report that these companies generally increased platinum output (both of plain metal jewellery and of gem-set pieces) over the end of 2011 and the start of 2012. Margins on platinum jewellery appear to have stabilised and we expect manufacturing output to climb by perhaps ten per cent this year. Unless metal prices rise sharply, the use of recycled metal seems to be relatively stable, suggesting that demand for fresh metal (i.e. the industry’s net demand) should climb fairly strongly too. The health of the palladium jewellery market continues to worsen. While there are still pockets of good retail demand within China (in Guangdong, Henan, Shandong and Szechuan provinces), sales are evidently much less strong than before, with demand in the North-East of the country where we had previously seen quantities of palladium on sale decreasing. This is reflected in our figure for manufacturing volumes (above) which

continue to show a substantial year-on-year fall. This is confirmed by lower working stocks of palladium (implying less throughput of material) and in lower finished stocks (implying less wholesaler and retailer demand). 

Manufacturer forecasts are for a further decline in palladium demand, although the rate of decline is expected to be lower than it has been in the last year or so. In our view, this is not related to the quality of palladium jewellery produced but rather to consumer awareness of palladium as a brand and movements in the bare metal price. 

More worrying for the state of the market is that margins on palladium jewellery have fallen once again. Looking back several years, there were considerably more palladium jewellery manufacturers active than is the case today. A shrinking market has encouraged many to end palladium production in favour of platinum, white gold or yellow gold. However, even with fewer manufacturers currently involved, there is still pressure on margins, suggesting that there is excess capacity. The use of recycled metal has also increased by a reasonable amount in the last year, with most of this coming from stocks of unsold jewellery, suggesting that consumer demand is still rather weak. 

### **The automotive sector** 

The slowing pace of the Chinese car market is concerning palladium investors as one of the pillars supporting strong fundamental demand is weakened. Sales of commercial and passenger vehicles fell by 3.4 per cent in the first quarter of 2012 compared to a year earlier. However, the signals from this market were a little mixed: passenger car sales fell only by 1.3 per cent to 3.77 million units in the quarter while March passenger car sales actually climbed by 4.5 per cent. As yet, there has been no attempt to downgrade the official growth target of between 8-10 per cent in new vehicle registrations. With a soft landing seemingly increasingly likely in China, we see some possibility that auto sales could fall below the bottom of this growth target but we feel that the downside is somewhat limited. 

It is, though, worth bearing in mind that the march of ever-tighter emissions legislation (and typical

ly higher platinum group metal loadings per car) continues. The Beijing Municipal Commission of Development and Reform announced that the Euro 5 equivalent Chinese rules will be implemented in Beijing ahead of the rest of the country and that it is planned to move to Euro 6 equivalent levels by 2016. However, in Russia, the Government was again forced to delay the domestic introduction of Euro 4 emissions rules which had been planned for 2012 until the start of 2013 due to a lack of high quality, low sulphur fuel. Euro 5 is now scheduled for implementation in 2015. Although the rules will not come into force as originally scheduled, there should be little short-tem impact on palladium demand: where manufacturers have already fitted higherloaded catalysts, they will not remove them simply because of a short term delay to the implementation of tighter limits. For unalloyed good news, though, it is worth looking towards the USA. There, buyers are spending record amount s of money on a typical new car as high used car prices make newer automobiles attractive. Improving economic conditions and general consumer sentiment are playing an important part too. Manufacturers have been confident enough to start reducing incentives for new purchasers too. New light duty vehicle sales reached a running rate of 15.1 million units in February and 14.4 million units in March, strongly up from annual sales of 12.8 million units sold last year. 22 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **19 April 2012** ### **Palladium investment** We continue to believe in the longer term attractions of palladium as an investment.
